title: Leadership Essentials: From Individual Contributor to Leader
summary: A comprehensive seven-module journey that guides you through the transition from individual contributor to effective leader. Learn to delegate strategically, coach for growth, build high-performing teams, make confident decisions, handle difficult conversations with grace, and develop the personal qualities that define great leaders.

modules.title: Module 1 • The Leadership Transition: From Doing to Leading
modules.overview: The transition from individual contributor to leader is one of the most challenging career moves. You're moving from being rewarded for what you do to being rewarded for what others achieve through you. This module helps you understand the fundamental shift in mindset, skills, and identity required for leadership. You'll learn to let go of doing and embrace leading. Great leaders aren't born—they're developed. This program gives you the framework and tools to become the leader you want to be.
takeaways: Leadership is a different job: it requires different skills, mindset, and focus than individual contribution.
Letting go of doing is essential: you can't lead effectively if you're still trying to do everything yourself.
Your success is now measured by your team's success: shift from 'I' to 'we'.
Leadership is learnable: with awareness, practice, and feedback, you can develop into an effective leader.
exercises: Mindset assessment: Reflect on your current mindset. Do you think like an individual contributor or a leader? Write down 3 examples of each mindset from your recent work.
Identity exploration: How do you see yourself? As an expert? As an enabler? As both? Write about how your identity needs to shift for leadership.
Pitfall audit: Which transition pitfalls do you recognize in yourself? Which ones are you most likely to fall into? Why?
homework: Leadership journal: This week, track when you think like an individual contributor vs. a leader. Note the situations and what you could do differently.
Mindset practice: Practice the leadership mindset in 3 situations this week. Instead of 'How can I solve this?' ask 'Who can solve this, and how can I help?'
Feedback request: Ask 2–3 team members for feedback on your leadership. What's working? What could improve? Listen without defending.
Transition plan: Create a personal transition plan. What individual contributor habits do you need to let go of? What leadership skills do you need to develop?

modules.title: Module 2 • Strategic Delegation: Multiplying Your Impact
modules.overview: Delegation is the superpower of leadership. When done well, it multiplies your impact, develops your team, and frees you to focus on what only you can do. Most new leaders struggle with delegation: they either delegate too little (micromanaging) or too much (dumping). This module teaches you to delegate strategically. You'll learn what to delegate, how to delegate effectively, and how to follow up without micromanaging.
takeaways: Delegation is not dumping: it's a strategic decision about who does what and why.
What you delegate matters more than how much: delegate the right things to the right people.
Clear expectations prevent problems: ambiguity is the enemy of effective delegation.
Follow-up is essential, but it's not micromanaging: check progress, provide support, but don't take over.
exercises: Delegation audit: List your current tasks. Which can you delegate? Which should you keep? Use the framework to decide.
Delegation practice: Delegate one task this week using the five-step process. Document what you did and how it went.
Expectation clarity: Review a recent delegation. Were expectations clear? What would you do differently?
homework: Delegation plan: Identify 3–5 tasks you can delegate. For each, identify: Who? Why them? What are the expectations? What's the authority? When are checkpoints?
Delegation execution: Delegate 2–3 tasks this week. Use the framework. Note what works and what doesn't.
Follow-up practice: Practice follow-up without micromanaging. Agree on checkpoints. Stick to them. Trust the process.
Delegation reflection: At the end of the week, reflect: What did you delegate? How did it go? What did you learn?

modules.title: Module 3 • Coaching for Growth: Developing Your Team
modules.overview: Great leaders are great coaches. They don't just tell people what to do—they help people discover how to do it better themselves. Coaching is different from managing. Managing is about getting work done. Coaching is about developing capability. You need both, but coaching is what creates lasting impact. This module teaches you the fundamentals of coaching: asking powerful questions, active listening, giving feedback, and creating development plans.
takeaways: Coaching develops capability: when you coach, you're building skills that last beyond the current task.
Questions are more powerful than answers: great coaches ask questions that help people discover solutions.
Feedback is a gift: when given well, it accelerates growth and builds trust.
Development is ongoing: coaching isn't a one-time event—it's a continuous practice.
exercises: GROW practice: Use the GROW model in one coaching conversation this week. Note what works and what's challenging.
Feedback practice: Give feedback using the SBI framework. Practice on a low-stakes situation first.
Development plan: Create a development plan for one team member. Use the framework. Get their input.
homework: Coaching commitment: Commit to one coaching conversation per week. Use GROW. Track what you learn.
Feedback log: Give 3 pieces of feedback this week using SBI. Note the response and impact.
Development plans: Create development plans for your team members. Review them together. Make them living documents.
Coaching reflection: Reflect on your coaching this week. What worked? What didn't? What will you do differently?

modules.title: Module 4 • Building High-Performing Teams: Trust and Collaboration
modules.overview: Great leaders build great teams. But teams don't just happen—they're built intentionally through trust, clear goals, effective processes, and strong relationships. This module teaches you to build teams that are more than the sum of their parts. You'll learn to create psychological safety, establish team norms, facilitate collaboration, and resolve conflicts. Team building isn't about team outings—it's about creating conditions where people can do their best work together.
takeaways: Trust is the foundation: without trust, teams can't function effectively.
Psychological safety enables performance: people need to feel safe to take risks, admit mistakes, and share ideas.
Clear goals and roles prevent conflict: ambiguity creates problems.
Great teams have great processes: how you work together matters as much as what you work on.
exercises: Trust assessment: Rate trust in your team 1–10. What's working? What's missing? What can you do to build more trust?
Psychological safety audit: How psychologically safe is your team? Can people speak up? Admit mistakes? Ask questions? What would make it safer?
Team norms creation: Facilitate a conversation to establish or review team norms. Get team input. Document agreements.
homework: Trust building: This week, take 3 actions to build trust: keep a commitment, admit a mistake, show care for someone. Note the impact.
Psychological safety practice: Create psychological safety in one interaction this week. Admit uncertainty, ask for feedback, respond non-defensively.
Collaboration facilitation: Facilitate one collaborative session this week. Set up the conditions. Step back. Let the team work.
Conflict resolution: If there's conflict in your team, address it this week. Use the framework. Work toward resolution.

modules.title: Module 5 • Confident Decision-Making: From Analysis to Action
modules.overview: Leaders make decisions constantly. Some are small and quick. Others are big and complex. Your ability to make good decisions efficiently is a core leadership skill. This module teaches you decision-making frameworks, helps you balance speed and quality, and gives you tools to make decisions confidently even with incomplete information. Great leaders don't wait for perfect information—they make the best decision they can with the information they have, then adjust as they learn more.
takeaways: Not all decisions are equal: use the right process for the right decision.
Speed matters: slow decisions can be as costly as bad decisions.
Involve the right people: some decisions need input, others need speed.
Decisions can be reversed: perfectionism paralyzes. Make the call, learn, adjust.
exercises: Decision audit: Review 5 recent decisions. Which were good? Which could have been better? What patterns do you notice?
Decision framework practice: Use the decision framework on a current decision. What type is it? What process should you use?
Speed vs. quality: Identify one decision you've been delaying. Use the framework. Make the call.
homework: Decision log: Track your decisions this week. Note: Type? Process? Speed? Quality? Outcome? What did you learn?
Decision practice: Make 3 decisions using the framework. One quick, one with input, one carefully considered. Note the differences.
Incomplete information: Make one decision with incomplete information this week. Use the framework. Monitor and adjust.
Decision communication: Practice communicating decisions clearly. Share: What? Why? What does it mean? What's next?

modules.title: Module 6 • Difficult Conversations: Leading Through Conflict
modules.overview: Difficult conversations are inevitable in leadership: giving feedback, addressing performance issues, handling conflicts, delivering bad news. How you handle them defines your leadership. Most leaders avoid difficult conversations because they're uncomfortable. But avoiding them makes problems worse. This module teaches you to have them well. You'll learn frameworks for difficult conversations, techniques for de-escalation, and skills for creating positive outcomes even from challenging situations.
takeaways: Difficult conversations are necessary: avoiding them makes problems worse.
Preparation enables confidence: knowing your framework reduces anxiety.
Focus on behavior, not character: address actions, not personality.
Seek to understand: most conflicts come from misunderstanding, not malice.
exercises: Difficult conversation preparation: Think of a difficult conversation you need to have. Use the framework to prepare. What's your purpose? What will you say?
SBI practice: Practice giving difficult feedback using SBI. Write it out. Refine it. Make it specific and actionable.
De-escalation practice: If you have a conflict, practice de-escalation techniques. Stay calm. Listen. Seek understanding.
homework: Difficult conversation: Have one difficult conversation this week. Prepare using the framework. Deliver it. Follow up. Note what works and what doesn't.
Feedback practice: Give 2–3 pieces of difficult feedback using SBI. Note the response and outcome.
Performance conversation: If you have a performance issue, address it this week. Use the framework. Document it.
Conflict resolution: If there's conflict in your team, facilitate resolution this week. Use de-escalation techniques. Work toward solutions.

modules.title: Module 7 • Personal Leadership Development: Becoming the Leader You Want to Be
modules.overview: This final module focuses on your personal development as a leader. Leadership isn't just about skills—it's about who you are, how you show up, and the impact you create. You'll develop your leadership philosophy, build self-awareness, create a development plan, and commit to practices that ensure continued growth. Great leaders are always learning. This module gives you the tools to continue growing throughout your leadership journey.
takeaways: Leadership is personal: your style should be authentic to you while incorporating best practices.
Self-awareness is foundational: you can't lead others well if you don't know yourself.
Continuous learning is essential: leadership mastery is a journey, not a destination.
Your development plan is your roadmap: use it to guide your growth.
exercises: Leadership philosophy: Write your leadership philosophy. What does leadership mean to you? What do you value? How do you want to lead?
Self-awareness assessment: Rate your self-awareness 1–10. What are your strengths? Weaknesses? Triggers? Patterns? What would you like to know better?
Development plan: Create your 90-day leadership development plan. What will you focus on? How will you practice? How will you measure progress?
homework: Philosophy refinement: Refine your leadership philosophy. Share it with someone. Get feedback. Make it clearer, more actionable.
Self-awareness practice: This week, practice self-awareness. Notice your patterns. Reflect on your leadership. Seek feedback.
Development plan creation: Create your comprehensive leadership development plan. Include strengths, growth areas, practices, and metrics. Review it weekly.
Habit building: Choose one leadership habit to build this week. Practice it daily. Track your progress. Make it stick.

aiSupport.systemPrompt: Help the user apply one concrete module step at a time. Do not diagnose. Escalate urgent safety concerns to emergency care.
